title: What is a feature flag — a way to turn features on/off without deploying new code (using tools like LaunchDarkly or simple config) — and why is it useful (test in production, gradual rollout, instant rollback)?
shortTitle: What a feature flag is and why it is useful

s1_definition.profdef: A feature flag (or feature toggle) is a runtime switch that decides whether a piece of functionality is active, allowing you to turn a feature on or off without deploying new code. Flags are evaluated at request time against configuration — held in a simple config, a database, or a dedicated service like LaunchDarkly or Unleash — so the same deployed binary can behave differently per environment, per user segment, or per percentage of traffic. This decouples deploying code from releasing a feature, enabling testing in production, gradual rollout, instant rollback by flipping the flag off, and targeted enablement for specific users.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of a feature flag at the National Bank of India as a light switch for a new service, wired in advance but kept off. The new instant-transfer feature is already built into the app and shipped to every branch, but the switch is off, so customers do not see it. The bank can flip it on just for Rajesh first, then for ten percent of customers, then everyone — and if something looks wrong, flip it straight off in seconds, with no need to send out a new app. The wiring (the deploy) and the switch (the release) are two separate actions.
s1_definition.oneliner: A feature flag is a runtime switch that turns functionality on or off without a redeploy, decoupling deployment from release so you can test in production, roll out gradually, and roll back instantly.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A feature flag (or feature toggle) is a runtime switch that decides whether a piece of functionality is active, allowing you to turn a feature on or off without deploying new code. Flags are evaluated at request time against configuration — held in a simple config, a database, or a dedicated service like LaunchDarkly or Unleash — so the same deployed binary can behave differently per environment, per user segment, or per percentage of traffic. This decouples deploying code from releasing a feature, enabling testing in production, gradual rollout, instant rollback by flipping the flag off, and targeted enablement for specific users.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of a feature flag at the National Bank of India as a light switch for a new service, wired in advance but kept off. The new instant-transfer feature is already built into the app and shipped to every branch, but the switch is off, so customers do not see it. The bank can flip it on just for Rajesh first, then for ten percent of customers, then everyone — and if something looks wrong, flip it straight off in seconds, with no need to send out a new app. The wiring (the deploy) and the switch (the release) are two separate actions.

**One line to remember:** A feature flag is a runtime switch that turns functionality on or off without a redeploy, decoupling deployment from release so you can test in production, roll out gradually, and roll back instantly.

sections.s2_technical:
At its simplest a feature flag is a boolean read at runtime: the code checks whether the flag is enabled and takes one path or the other. The flag value comes from a source that can change without redeploying — an environment variable or config file for basic cases, a database or config service for dynamic changes, or a dedicated platform like LaunchDarkly, Unleash, or Flagsmith for advanced targeting. The crucial property is that flipping the flag does not require shipping new code; the binary already contains both paths, and the flag selects which one runs. This is why flags decouple deployment from release: you can deploy code with a feature dark and release it later by flipping the switch.

Flags come in several kinds. A release flag gradually exposes a new feature and is removed once the feature is fully rolled out. An operational or kill-switch flag lets you disable an expensive or risky subsystem instantly under load, for example turning off a heavy recommendation call during a traffic spike. An experiment flag drives A/B tests by splitting users into variants and measuring outcomes. A permission flag enables a feature only for specific user segments, such as premium customers or internal beta testers. Good flag systems evaluate rules — percentage rollouts, user attributes, environment — so the same flag can be on for one percent of traffic, or only for users in a particular segment, or only in staging.

The benefits are concrete. Testing in production becomes safe because you can enable a feature only for internal users or a tiny percentage and observe real behavior with real data before a wide release. Gradual rollout lets you increase exposure step by step while watching metrics, which limits blast radius much like a canary but at the feature level rather than the deployment level. Instant rollback is the standout benefit: if a feature misbehaves, flipping the flag off disables it in seconds without a redeploy or a rollback pipeline, which is far faster than reverting a release. Flags also enable trunk-based development, where incomplete features are merged behind a flag that is off, so the team avoids long-lived branches while keeping unfinished work invisible to users.

There are costs and senior nuances. Flags add conditional branches, so unmanaged flags accumulate into technical debt and make code harder to reason about; the discipline is to remove release flags promptly once a feature is fully live and to keep a registry of active flags with owners and expiry. Flag evaluation must be fast and resilient — you cache values and define a safe default so an outage of the flag service does not break requests. In a bank you also audit flag changes, because flipping a flag is effectively a production change that can alter how money moves, and you guard sensitive flags with approvals. Finally, flags should be evaluated consistently for a given user so a customer does not flicker between old and new behavior, which is achieved by hashing the user identifier into a stable bucket.
sections.s3_banking:
The National Bank of India is launching an instant-transfer feature. It is risky, so it must ship dark, be enabled for internal users first, then a growing percentage, and be instantly disable-able via a kill switch — all without redeploying.

Problem 1 — The feature is already built and deployed but must stay invisible until the bank is confident. A flag that defaults off ships the code dark and releases it later.

Problem 2 — The bank wants to enable it for Rajesh (an internal beta user) first, then ten percent of customers, then everyone, consistently per user. A percentage-plus-segment rule with stable per-user bucketing achieves this.

Problem 3 — If the feature misbehaves, the bank must disable it in seconds. A kill switch flipped off does that with no redeploy. Our runnable Java simulation models a `FeatureFlag` evaluated against a `FlagContext` (user, segment) with percentage rollout, segment targeting, and a kill switch, plus a `TransferService` whose behavior depends on the flag. Classes: `FlagContext`, `FeatureFlag`, `FeatureFlagService`, `TransferService`, and a `FeatureFlagDemo` main.

##### 4c. Flag Configuration (YAML)

```yaml
# ─── File: config/flags.yaml ───
# Simple config-based flags (equivalent concept to LaunchDarkly rules).
instant-transfer:
  killSwitch: false          # flip true to disable INSTANTLY, no redeploy
  rolloutPercentage: 10      # 10% of customers (stable per-user bucket)
  enabledSegments: [internal-beta]   # always on for internal beta users
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Run the Java demo
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -cp target/classes com.bank.flags.FeatureFlagDemo

# With a real flag service (LaunchDarkly concept)
# flags are flipped in the dashboard / API — the running app picks them up live:
curl -X PATCH https://flags.nbi.in/api/flags/instant-transfer \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"killSwitch": true}'   # instant global off
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: the instant-transfer flag shipped dark with a ten percent rollout and the internal-beta segment enabled, evaluated for Rajesh (internal-beta) and Priya (retail).

Step 1 — Rajesh initiates a transfer. The flag service sees his segment is internal-beta, which is in the enabled segments, so the feature is on for him and he takes the new instant path, even though the overall rollout is only ten percent.

Step 2 — Priya initiates a transfer. She is retail, not a targeted segment, so the service hashes her user identifier into a stable bucket from 0 to 99 and compares it to the ten percent threshold. Suppose her bucket is above ten, so the feature is off for her and she takes the standard batch path.

Step 3 — The bank widens the rollout to one hundred percent by changing the flag value at runtime, with no redeploy. Priya transfers again, and now her bucket is below one hundred, so she takes the new instant path.

Step 4 — An incident occurs, so an operator flips the kill switch on. On the next evaluations for both Rajesh and Priya, the kill switch short-circuits everything and the feature is off for everyone, so both fall back to the standard path immediately — all without shipping new code.

Step 5 — The journey shows the three superpowers of flags: targeted enablement for a segment, consistent percentage rollout per user, and instant global disable via the kill switch, each achieved by changing configuration rather than redeploying.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 02:55:00 [INFO   ] === Dark launch: 10% rollout + internal-beta segment ===
2026-10-30 02:55:00 [INFO   ] instant-transfer ON for SAV2001 via segment internal-beta
2026-10-30 02:55:00 [INFO   ] INSTANT transfer Rs.50000 SAV2001→CUR3001 for SAV2001 (new path)
2026-10-30 02:55:00 [INFO   ] instant-transfer OFF for CUR3001 (bucket 47 vs 10%)
2026-10-30 02:55:00 [INFO   ] STANDARD (T+0 batch) transfer Rs.20000 CUR3001→SAV2001 for CUR3001 (old path)
2026-10-30 02:55:00 [INFO   ] === Widen rollout to 100% (no redeploy) ===
2026-10-30 02:55:00 [INFO   ] instant-transfer ON for CUR3001 (bucket 47 vs 100%)
2026-10-30 02:55:00 [INFO   ] INSTANT transfer Rs.20000 CUR3001→SAV2001 for CUR3001 (new path)
2026-10-30 02:55:00 [INFO   ] === Incident! Flip KILL SWITCH off (instant, no redeploy) ===
2026-10-30 02:55:00 [WARNING] instant-transfer KILL SWITCH ON — disabled for everyone
2026-10-30 02:55:00 [INFO   ] STANDARD (T+0 batch) transfer Rs.50000 SAV2001→CUR3001 for SAV2001 (old path)
2026-10-30 02:55:00 [WARNING] instant-transfer KILL SWITCH ON — disabled for everyone
2026-10-30 02:55:00 [INFO   ] STANDARD (T+0 batch) transfer Rs.20000 CUR3001→SAV2001 for CUR3001 (old path)
```


sections.s6_takeaway:
A feature flag is a runtime switch that decides whether a piece of functionality is active, so I can turn a feature on or off without deploying new code. The flag value is read at request time from a source that can change without a redeploy — a config file for simple cases, or a dedicated service like LaunchDarkly or Unleash for advanced targeting — and because the deployed binary already contains both code paths, flipping the flag just selects which one runs. The fundamental idea is that it decouples deploying code from releasing a feature: I can ship code dark and release it later by flipping the switch.

This gives three concrete benefits. Testing in production becomes safe because I can enable a feature only for internal users or a tiny percentage and watch real behavior with real data before a wide release. Gradual rollout lets me increase exposure step by step while watching metrics, which limits blast radius at the feature level much like a canary does at the deployment level. And instant rollback is the standout benefit: if a feature misbehaves, I flip the flag off and it is disabled in seconds, with no redeploy and no rollback pipeline, which is far faster than reverting a release. Flags also enable trunk-based development, since unfinished work can be merged behind a flag that is off, avoiding long-lived branches.

In my project at the National Bank of India we launched instant transfer behind a flag: it shipped dark, was enabled first for internal beta users like Rajesh, then for ten percent of customers with a stable per-user bucket so no one flickered between old and new behavior, then widened to everyone by changing the config at runtime — and when an incident occurred, an operator flipped the kill switch and the feature went off for everyone instantly without any deploy. A senior point I always add is that flags are a production change that can alter how money moves, so I audit flag changes and guard sensitive ones with approvals, I cache flag values with a safe default so a flag-service outage does not break requests, and I remove release flags promptly once a feature is fully live, because unmanaged flags accumulate into technical debt. Used with that discipline, feature flags are one of the most powerful tools for shipping safely.
